items.titleRaw: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs
items.contentRaw: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.

payloadJson.title: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs

items.titleRaw: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
items.contentRaw: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

payloadJson.title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery

items.titleRaw: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
items.contentRaw: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.

payloadJson.title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking

items.titleRaw: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
items.contentRaw: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank. To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost. UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (<=33.3%).

payloadJson.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control

items.titleRaw: Industrial ReMEmbR: Scaling Spatiotemporal Memory to Robot Fleets
items.contentRaw: Warehouse robot fleets continuously observe operational conditions, but preserving these observations as reusable semantic memory incurs substantial computation, communication, and storage costs. For example, explaining recurring aisle blockages can require reviewing video from multiple robots across several shifts. We present IndustrialRemembr, a shared spatiotemporal memory system that extends NVIDIA ReMEmbR to robot fleets and reduces server-side computation by generating scene descriptions only on demand. On each robot, an NVIDIA Jetson encodes video clips into retrieval embeddings with Cosmos-Embed1, vision tokens with Cosmos3-Edge, and reconstruction latents with the Wan2.2 VAE, without uploading raw camera frames. The encoding models are re-used to detect people in image patches, zeroing them out to support PII abstraction for GDPR-compliant deployments. We split Cosmos3-Edge at its vision-language boundary, placing the vision encoder on the robot and the language decoder on an on-premises server. A Nemotron agent retrieves memories by content, position, and time and queries the decoder using cached vision tokens. This design eliminates caption generation at write time, while cached-token decoding reproduces the unsplit model's output in all 450 tested decodes.

payloadJson.title: Industrial ReMEmbR: Scaling Spatiotemporal Memory to Robot Fleets

items.titleRaw: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
items.contentRaw: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

payloadJson.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators

items.titleRaw: anthropics/claude-code v2.1.305 released
items.contentRaw:
## What's changed

- Added `sandbox.allowNestedUserNamespaces` so sandboxed commands on Linux can create user namespaces (Chromium, rootless podman); this lets them get around the sandbox's file protections
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG_USAGE_LIMIT_RECHECK_MS` so unattended retry mode (`CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG`) notices a usage limit that was lifted before its reset
- Fixed every request failing on Vertex, Bedrock and other providers when the endpoint or a gateway rejects tool search, and behind gateways with ToolSearch disallowed or left out of `--tools` (a 2.1.304 regression): Claude Code now retries without it
- Fixed `/effort` and `/autocompact` settings not applying when the model name differed from a `modelOverrides` value by letter case or a `[1m]` tag
- Fixed new worktrees in a bare repository sometimes starting from local HEAD instead of the default branch, and unchanged subagent worktrees sometimes not being cleaned up
- Fixed Bash commands on a full disk failing with a raw `ENOSPC` file path: the error now says the disk is full and that nothing ran
- Fixed an MCP server passed by a cloud session or by the SDK's `setMcpServers` being replaced later in the session by a same-named server from your own settings
- Fixed Claude naming the wrong model for a subagent's work after the subagent switched to a fallback model
- Fixed cloud sessions and teammates not telling Claude when a compaction had to leave the oldest messages out of its summary to fit
- Fixed more cases of scheduled Cowork cloud sessions waiting five minutes for each subagent whose WebFetch needed a URL approval that nobody was there to give
- Fixed Workflow resume re-running already-completed `pipeline()` and `parallel()` agents instead of serving them from the run's journal
- Fixed Remote Control leaving empty "(session)" entries in `/resume` after switching conversations with `/resume`
- Fixed `/usage` rows being cut off in narrow terminals
- Fixed startup warnings printing as raw text above the logo: they now go to the debug log, and permission rules that restrict nothing show as warning rows under the banner
- Fixed screen reader mode: search boxes now say "Search:" instead of a symbol VoiceOver read as "telephone recorder", and highlighted prompt text, such as Ctrl+R search matches and "ultrathink", no longer has spaces inside words
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed a start script that shares only its stdout with the runner or orchestrator failing with `Resource temporarily unavailable` when `TERM` is set (a 2.1.300 regression)
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed repository access failing since 2.1.296 when a git credential helper or askpass program reads its settings through `GIT_CONFIG`
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed the orchestrator reporting a spawn-runner hook as timed out when a runner it started in the background kept its output open
- Improved `/usage`: each warning is now a one-line fix that names its source, and `f` applies the fixes; the same fixes appear in VS Code and `/doctor`
- Improved MCP consent dialogs so an Enter meant for the prompt is less likely to be taken as Accept
- Improved a mod's `Image` to draw its picture in iTerm2 3.5 and later with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its `alt` text
- Remote Control: Improved the spawn-mode messages: pressing `w` now says the new mode is saved for the folder, and a later `claude remote-control` start that uses the saved mode says where it came from
- Changed `allowedMcpServers` to stop filtering `managed-mcp.json` stdio servers that use `${VAR}` only in `env`: one your allowlist left out now loads on upgrade; use `deniedMcpServers` to keep it off
- Changed plugins that Claude Desktop mounts by path to no longer keep their `allowed-tools` when your organization's managed settings set `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`
- Changed the `/artifacts` delete confirmation to take 1 or Enter to keep, 2 to delete, and Esc to cancel; `y` and `n` no longer answer it
- Changed a mod's docked pane to stay within 45% of the terminal's width, including a width kept from a wider terminal
- [VSCode] Added a "Running start-up hooks" spinner status, with a screen reader announcement, while SessionStart or Setup hooks run
- [VSCode] Fixed the spinner cutting off "Compacting..." when your `spinnerVerbs` setting replaces the built-in verbs with short ones
- [VSCode] Changed the message shown when a session does not start in time and no hook is running: it now leads with the output logs and lists causes instead of pointing to sign-in and network first
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed the Cloud environments admin page wrongly refusing to save an existing environment with an "installs packages" error
- [Cloud sessions] Improved deleting a self-hosted environment so the dialog and error messages say what blocks the delete and what it will affect
- [Claude Tag] Added public Slack channels Claude hasn't joined to the Claude Tag admin Add place search, so admins can set one up from there
- [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude Tag access bundles so a repository that moved to another GitHub account can be added again
- [Claude Tag] Fixed a routine set up in a Slack DM thread no longer posting after another routine in that thread restarted the conversation; both now keep posting there
- [Claude Tag] Fixed routines set up in a Slack thread reporting success without posting after the conversation ended; those runs are now skipped and the creator is told
- [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag admin pages in large organizations so plugin, skill and bundle edits work while the channel list is still loading
- [Code Review] Fixed Code Review sometimes not reviewing the newest commit when several pushes landed on a pull request during a review
- [Code Review] Changed Code Review re-reviews so they no longer open with LGTM while earlier blocking findings are still open

items.titleRaw: huggingface/transformers v5.20.0 released
items.contentRaw: # Release v5.20.0 ## New Model additions ### Muse Spark Open Muse Spark Open is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta that takes text, images, audio, and video as input and generates text. It has 816B total parameters (42B active per token) and a context window of up to 1,048,576 tokens shared across modalities. It is trained for agentic coding tasks such as multi-file editing, debugging, and tool use. Checkpoints are available in BF16 and NVFP4 formats. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/muse_spark) | [Blog Post](http://hf.co/blog/meta-muse-spark-open) * Add Muse Spark Open (#49644) by @guarin in [#49644](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49644) ### Ling 3.0 Ling 3.0 Flash is a hybrid Mixture-of-Experts language model from InclusionAI. Its decoder groups five Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) layers with one Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) layer. The MLA blocks use interleaved rotary embeddings and a head-wise output gate, and the feed-forward blocks combine routed and shared experts. It is natively supported in Transformers as `BailingHybridForCausalLM`, so it loads without `trust_remote_code=True`. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/bailing_hybrid) * [Model] Add native Ling 3.0 Flash support (#49446) by @icavan in [#49446](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49446) ### Kolibri1 Kolibri 1 is Aleph Alpha's mixture-of-experts reasoning model, focused on German and English. items.contentRaw: # Release v5.19.0 ## New Model additions ### EmbeddingGemma2 EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model from Google built on the Gemma 4 architecture. It encodes text, images, audio, and video, individually or combined in one input, into a shared 768-dimensional vector space for cross-modal retrieval, semantic similarity, clustering, and classification. It uses Matryoshka Representation Learning, so embeddings can be truncated to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions. It also offers configurable visual and video token budgets, and unused vision or audio towers can be disabled at load time to save memory. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/embedding_gemma2) * Smthn smthn (#49364) by @vasqu in [#49364](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49364) ## Breaking changes All MoE models whose routers compute logits now return them when `output_router_logits=True`, following the Qwen3-MoE pattern (a `router_logits` recorder on the base model, `MoeModelOutputWithPast` from the backbone, and a MoE causal LM output from the head), so code that relied on the previous outputs or their absence should read the router logits from these output classes. * 🚨 Return router logits from every MoE model that computes them (#48920) by @qgallouedec `Owlv2ForObjectDetection.embed_image_query` now selects the query box with the highest objectness score, as in the original OWLv2 notebook, instead of the OWL-ViT heuristic, so image-guided query embeddings and detections may differ from earlier releases. * 🚨 Select the OWLv2 image query by objectness (#49200) by @qgallouedec The `"paged|"` prefix for SDPA and flash attention implementations is deprecated, so users should set the regular attention implementation (e.g. `sdpa` or `flash_attention_2`) for continuous batching instead of `paged|sdpa` or `paged|flash_attention_2`. * 🚨 Attention 🚨 Deprecate "paged|" prefix for SDPA and flash (#49112) by @remi-or The regular flash and SDPA attention functions (`flash_attention.py`, `sdpa_attention.py`) now support continuous batching directly, and `"paged|..."` implementations for these are redirected to them, while eager still requires the `"paged|eager"` prefix. * 🚨 Attention 🚨 Make regular attention support CB (#49101) by @remi-or In continuous batching, the cache update for the index-based and block-table paths is now fused into a single call, which slightly changes the cache update function's behavior and affects any custom code that calls the separate update paths. * 🚨 [CB] 🚨 Fuse update for index and block table path (#49088) by @remi-or Continuous batching internals changed in preparation for removing `"paged"`: `max * 🚨 [CB] 🚨 Little fixes before removing "paged" (#49069) by @remi-or ## Parallelization Expert parallelism gains a token-dispatch implementation, selected via the new `ep_dispatch_experts` plan rule and now the default for Qwen3 MoE and Mellum, which removes the requirement that EP size equal TP size. The `Trainer` was also adapted to work with expert parallelism, and the docs now note that PEFT adapters support tensor parallelism. A CI-related fix for pipeline-parallel chart2table inference was also included. * [`distributed`]: adapt Trainer to work Expert Parallel (#48873) by @3outeille in [#48873] * [`distributed`] Add expert-parallel token dispatch, default for Qwen3 MoE (#48865) by @3outeille in [#48865] * Fix pp chart2table inference (#49225) by @zucchini-nlp in [#49225] * [docs] TP for PEFT adapters (#49060) by @stevhliu in [#49060] ## Cache This release fixes quantized cache handling: `generate` no longer mutates the user's `cache_config`, and `QuantizedLayer.reorder_cache` is repaired. It also adds per-layer cache configuration, so `DynamicCache` and `StaticCache` initialize each layer from its own config (sliding window, attention chunk size, conv states, and attention head counts) to better support heterogeneous models. ## What's Changed
* [pplx-decider](https://ollama.com/library/pplx-decider) is a 27B decision model from Perplexity, fine-tuned from
Qwen3.8-27B
* Continuing an OpenAI-compatible Responses conversation no longer fails when switching between models with and without
thinking, or when the history contains another provider's compaction items
* Fixed streaming Responses requests where client tool calls (e.g. Codex with web search) could emit before open
reasoning items, producing misordered/duplicate tool call events
* Requests routed to remote models are now cancelled on ollama.com when the client disconnects, instead of continuing
to run
* `ollama show` now reports which renderer and parser a model uses and where its chat template comes from; the API
exposes the same values in new `renderer`, `parser`, and `template_source` fields
* More draft models now work with speculative decoding: llama-server infers the draft type automatically instead of
requiring Ollama to identify it
* `ollama launch claude` now clamps `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW` to Claude Code's supported range, avoiding a
"window too large" warning
* Updated llama.cpp and MLX

## NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super

[NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super](https://ollama.com/library/nemotron-3.5-super) is a vision-language model for coding, reasoning, tool use, and document understanding. It pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mamba-2/Transformer mixture-of-experts backbone (12B active per token) with a C-RADIO vision encoder, and supports tool calling, an on/off thinking mode, and context up to 1M tokens.


items.titleRaw: Show HN: AgentState – Lightweight state manager for multi-agent AI workflows
items.contentRaw:
AgentState to solve a problem I kept running into: managing state for multi-agent AI systems is surprisingly hard. When you have multiple AI agents that need to coordinate, persist their state, and query each other's status, you typically end up with a mess of Redis/Postgres setups, custom queuing, and manual synchronization code.

The whole thing is ~3MB, written in Rust for performance and safety, runs in Docker, and handles 1000+ ops/sec. I've been running it in production for AI workflows and it's been rock solid.

items.titleRaw: Show HN: ML Blocks – Deploy multimodal AI workflows without code
items.contentRaw:
Hey everyone,

ML Blocks is a node-based workflow builder to create multi-modal AI workflows without writing any code.

You connect blocks that call various visual models like GPT4v, Segment Anything, Dino etc. along with basic image processing blocks like resize, invert color, blur, crop, and several others.

The idea is to make it easier to deploy multi-step image processing workflows, without needing to spin up endless custom OpenCV cloud functions to glue together AI models. Usually, even if you're using cloud inference servers like Replicate, you still need to write your own image processing code to pre and post-process images in your pipeline. When you're trying to move fast, that's just unnecessary overhead.

With ML Blocks, you can build a workflow and deploy the whole thing as a single API. AFAIK, ML Blocks is the only end-to-end workflow builder built specifically for image processing.

If you're curious, our models run on Replicate, HuggingFace & Modal Labs cloud GPUs and we use React Flow for the node UX.
